A traditional East Asian ink-wash painting (sumi-e) on one plain sheet of warm, light rice paper with fine fibres, seen flat from straight above, evenly lit, no shadow, no frame, no table, no text, no signature, no red seal, no stamp. Paint it the way a master ink painter works: a few confident, loose brush strokes, wet ink bleeding softly into the paper, dry-brush texture where the brush runs out, simplified forms that suggest rather than describe, lots of white paper. It must look like a painting, expressive and artistic, with the brushwork of the reference picture: never a realistic drawing, never a detailed illustration, never a pencil sketch, never a 3D render. Copy only the reference's brushwork, never its subject: no bird, no crane, no reeds. Sumi ink only, from deep black to soft grey washes, plus real gold leaf only where stated. Generous empty paper on every side. The subject fills most of the picture. The picture is a long, low strip: the things named sit in a band across the middle, with plain paper above and below them and soft, misty ends on the left and right. Only the things named below are painted: no landscape, no mountains, no pine trees, no floor, no wall, no people.

A long, simple low wooden shelf seen from the front, painted in a few dry-brush strokes, holding many rolled handscrolls lying on their sides, stacked two and three high along its whole length, each tied with a thin cord, their round ends facing us as loose ink circles. Near the middle, three scrolls have been pulled forward and lie on the front edge of the shelf, a little apart from the rest; one of the three is partly unrolled, showing a short stretch of paper with a few faint, illegible lines of ink. Calm and orderly, a scholar's library of scrolls. Ink only, no gold.
